blocks.text: For Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 667 f., חגב is the fourth kind of locust, i.e. the locust of the fourth and last stage, named from حجب [ḥjb], to veil, because, once it flies, it veils the sun and the sky. Tychsen, however, p. 76 ff., considers חגב to be the same locust as the gryllus coronatus Linn., which received its name from veiling on account of the length of its wings. Since חגב is sometimes used in figurative speech to express the worthlessness and smallness of something (see Num. XIII, 34. Esaj. XL, 22.), to Oedmann, p. 90, 91, it seems to be some smaller species of locust.

R. Jonah, or Abu'l-Walid, renders חנמל in the same way in his unpublished Lexicon, as Schnurrer reports in his Dissertation on Psalm 78 (which is included in the Commentatt. Theologg. edited by Velthusen, Kuinoel and Ruperti, vol. 1, p. 76 f.), in the note on v. 47.

Michaelis in the Supplemm. p. 846 holds that חנמל are larger ants, a quadriliteral formed from נמלה, ant, with the letter Chet prefixed, which (to use Schnurrer's words, loc. cit.) we fear will not win the approval of many. Paulus in the Clavis Psalmorum p. 198 suspects that two words, חן, compare Arabic حُنَن [ḥunan] dung beetle, and מל, compare مُلل [mulal] dried out by heat, have been joined into the single word חנמל.

Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 862 ff. thinks the meaning locust must be rejected chiefly because חסיל is distinguished from ארבה in I Reg. VIII, 37. Ioel. I, 4. II, 25. But what if different species of locusts are designated by these words? And that this is truly so appears from Psal. LXXVIII, 46., where חסיל is parallel to ארבה, the best-known name of the locust, and from Ies. XXXIII, 4., where חסילים correspond to גבים in the other member and are said to be gathered together with them, as we shall explain more fully below on Chapter 2. Michaelis himself, however, wavers between the gryllo-talpa, or cricket with mole's feet (in German Maulwurfs-Grille, Rietwurm), which is destructive to crops, and the bruchus, which would be called חסיל, adult, from חסל, to complete, transferred to adult age. For the gryllo-talpa he adduces the Syriac translator, who in Joel has ܢܘܣܠܐ, cricket (which, however, Michaelis refers to the gryllo-talpa without adequate reason); for the bruchus, the Vulgate, the Alexandrian translator at 2 Paral. VI, 28., and Aquila at Ps. LXXVIII, 46. Michaelis's opinion about the gryllo-talpa is refuted at length by Oedmann, fasc. 2, ch. 6, p. 138 ff., for whom חסיל is the cimex Aegyptius Linn., on the authority of the Arabic translator, who puts قمل [qaml], which he takes to be the name of the bug. Tychsen, p. 91, 92, interprets חסיל as the gryllus verrucivorus Linn. (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 4, p. 2067), relying on the meaning of the verb חסל, he consumed entirely. How uncertain this is anyone will see for himself, since this etymology fits almost all species of locusts. Paulus in the Clavis Psalmorum p. 197 thinks that חסיל is a caterpillar that has crept out of the nymph, or larva, [III, 257] compare Arabic خشل [khshl], he rejected it as rather worthless, a garment was worn out. Why I think the locust is to be understood I have already said above; but the species no one could determine today.

For the Arabs حرجل [ḥarjal] is not only a swarm of locusts, but also a wingless kind of locust, Gryllus onos or papus, Linn. (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 4, p. 2068, 69), the same that, on the testimony of Dioscorides, was called ἀσίρακος [asirakos] around Leptis in Africa (עסקרא, عسكر [ʿaskar], pedestrian); see Bochart below, p. 450. Adderaihem in Casiri, Biblioth. Arab. Hisp. vol. 1, p. 320 a, confirms the same. Compare Hyde in the Notes on Peritsol's Itinera mundi, p. 125. Damir, however, does not even have the name حرجل [ḥarjal], as Tychsen reports, p. 73. Michaelis in the Supplemm. p. 911 thinks the wingless kind of locust is no different from locusts not yet winged, a strange error, since there are several species of locusts that lack wings entirely, such as Gryllus papus, spinulosus, pedestris, onos, Linn. From the sequence of the passage Levit. XI, 22., חרגל for Michaelis is the locust not yet winged, after the third shedding of its skin. He thinks the name חרגל is compounded from the Samaritan רגולה, pedestrian, and the Arabic خرج [kharaja], he went out, so that by etymology חרגל would be the pedestrian locust (creeping on the ground, as opposed to the winged one) that has come out of its skins after the third shedding. For Tychsen, p. 74, חרגל is the gryllus gurges of Asso, related to the gryllus verrucivorus Linn. Mere conjectures!
